conflicts.point: Whether a training-run origin defect that produces individually bounded but perfectly origin-correlated losses across all licensees draws an outright reinsurance exclusion or instead a priced uncertainty margin.

positions.stance: Bounded in-scope harms aggregate the way earthquake clash and pandemic business-interruption do; the reinsurance market loads them with capital charges and layered attachments, so strict exposure adds no distinct work; refusal to write occurs only at the systemic tail the topic excludes.

A single opaque training run replicated across licensees lacks the base rate, diversification, and loss history that let reinsurers bound a catastrophe book; with no independence across insureds the loss draws an origin-exclusion clause, as existing errors-and-omissions and technology-liability policies already carve out algorithmic bias and systemic model error.

conflicts.point: Whether assigning the cost of an unresolved epistemic gap to the developer who controlled the evidence constitutes principled allocation or an undifferentiated levy on uncertainty.

positions.stance: The developer and victim are not symmetric: one party could have generated the missing data and profited from not doing so, while the other could not have generated it at any price, so placing the cost on the evidence-controller mirrors the century-old product-liability principle that keeps manufacturers from converting their own opacity into the consumer's loss.

Dodging the classification step does not resolve the missing data; it taxes the developer for it, converting an epistemic gap into a balance-sheet penalty levied on the one party whose foreseeability is the contested object, which is the chilling residual relocated to a cleaner address.

conflicts.point: Whether the developer-side coverage gate, priced off the disclosed red-team log, actually reaches the upstream design-defect risk or merely prices the tested subset and writes the seam out through exclusion.

positions.stance: A release-gate requiring third-party coverage priced off disclosed testing forces the underwriter to rate the training run directly and triggers reinsurance recourse upstream, closing the seam without a strict-liability default.

The gate prices off a log that is silent on the untested surface, so it prices only the probed subset and writes broad exclusions over the design-defect risk that generated the seam; a broad exclusion is the seam priced out, not coverage of it.

conflicts.point: Whether the strategic-ignorance versus genuine-unforeseeability line, undrawable by the evidence-holder before harm, is nonetheless decidable ex post from dated disclosure records.

positions.stance: The log proves only the tested space and is silent on the untested-but-should-have-been-tested space; making a thin log probative requires ruling that the absence of a test was itself negligent, which reintroduces the hindsight-bias judgment for which no inter-rater reliability data exists.

Undrawable by the evidence-holder before the harm is not the same as undecidable in principle; a dated red-team coverage log shrinks the hindsight window by putting pre-harm testing scope on the record, so the line is drawable ex post.

verdicts.conflict: Whether a correlated training-run defect across all licensees draws a reinsurance origin-exclusion or a priced uncertainty margin.
verdicts.rationale: C25 cites existing E&O and technology-liability policies that already carve out algorithmic bias and systemic model error, an observable current-market artifact, and identifies the specific missing inputs reinsurers require: base rate, diversification, and loss history. C26 offers analogies to earthquake clash and pandemic business-interruption but those perils retain geographic or temporal independence that a single replicated training run lacks, so the analogy weakens on the precise feature at issue.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence of an actual reinsurance treaty pricing correlated model-origin losses through layered attachment rather than excluding them would flip the verdict toward C26.

verdicts.conflict: Whether assigning epistemic-gap cost to the evidence-controlling developer is principled allocation or an undifferentiated uncertainty tax.
verdicts.rationale: C27 grounds allocation in a stated asymmetry — one party could have generated the missing data and profited from withholding it, the other could not at any price — which maps onto a documented century-long product-liability principle. C29 correctly notes the allocation does not manufacture the missing data, but that observation does not defeat the fairness argument, since allocation rules operate precisely when facts are unrecoverable; C29's 'contested object' framing assumes the conclusion that foreseeability is genuinely indeterminate, which the disclosure mechanism in C11 disputes.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A showing that developers cannot in fact generate the relevant data at feasible cost would collapse the asymmetry and strengthen C29's tax characterization.

verdicts.conflict: Whether a coverage gate priced off the red-team log reaches upstream design-defect risk or only prices the tested subset and excludes the seam.
verdicts.rationale: C18 rests on a definitional point that is hard to rebut: a testing log is silent by construction about what was not tested, so a rate priced off it cannot cover the untested surface without a further assumption. C21 asserts the gate 'forces the underwriter to rate the training run directly,' but does not explain how an underwriter prices a failure mode absent from the disclosed evidence, leaving the exclusion mechanism C18 describes unaddressed.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: An underwriting practice that prices untested-surface risk through a loaded uncertainty margin rather than an exclusion — demonstrated in a real policy — would support C21.

verdicts.conflict: Whether the strategic-ignorance versus genuine-unforeseeability line, undrawable ex ante, is nonetheless decidable ex post from dated disclosure records.
verdicts.rationale: C14 correctly distinguishes 'undrawable before harm by the evidence-holder' from 'undecidable in principle,' and timestamped logs do shrink the hindsight window by fixing pre-harm testing scope on the record. But C12 identifies a genuine gap C14 does not fill: deciding that the absence of a test was itself negligent still requires a judgment for which no inter-rater reliability data exists, and a dated log constrains but does not eliminate that judgment.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Inter-rater reliability studies showing that reviewers converge on 'this untested surface should have been tested' given standardized logs would resolve toward C14; wide reviewer divergence would confirm C12.

verdicts.conflict: Whether insurer repricing at renewal disciplines developer conduct better than a tort standard, given that the actuarial engine ingests only filed, attributed claims.
verdicts.rationale: C5 is supported by real experience-rated markets in cyber, commercial-auto, and professional liability, which is strong evidence that repricing disciplines conduct. But C20 identifies a concrete structural gap: the premium-payer is usually the deployer, while the design defect sits upstream with the developer whose choices the deployer's insurer never rates, so repricing the deployer never touches the training run. C7 reinforces that the engine cannot reach unlitigated harms; together they bound C5's mechanism rather than defeat it.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that developer-side coverage gates (C30) are actually written and priced against training-run testing in practice would close the seam C20 identifies and strengthen C5.

verdicts.conflict: Whether negligence fails to attach at all for genuinely emergent AI behavior, and whether product-liability precedent justifies strict liability for diffuse AI harms.
verdicts.rationale: C1 and C2 make a coherent case that negligence cannot attach where no breachable duty exists and that courts historically migrated to strict liability under exactly that condition. C3 correctly limits the precedent to concrete, attributable, physically injurious harms, and C4 reframes strict liability as a deployment tax rather than deterrence when no care level existed to incentivize. C15 subsumes all of these by relocating the constraint to disclosure — showing that foreseeability is not fixed but a function of who holds evidence — which accounts for both the safetyist's attachment problem and the accelerationist's deterrence objection.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that bias audits and mandatory disclosure do not in fact make foreseeability determinable outside a courtroom would undercut C15 and return the contest to C1 versus C3/C4.
